analysis.one_liner: Cuts capital gains taxes to 15 percent and makes 2001 tax cuts permanent.
analysis.headline: Representative Pat Toomey's bill to cut the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and permanently extend the 2001 Bush tax cuts never got a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would slash the top tax rate on profits from selling stocks and other investments to 15 percent, repeal the exclusion for small business stock gains, and repeal the built-in expiration dates of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, making its tax cuts permanent, including the higher education tuition deduction, the saver's credit, and the alternative minimum tax exemption increase [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Mainly wealthy households and investors who realize large capital gains, who would pay a top rate of 15 percent on investment profits instead of 20 percent [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a maximum 15 percent rate on individual net capital gains, with a 7.5 percent rate on gains within the lower brackets, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2001 [S3].
Repeals title IX of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, the compliance provision that caused its tax cuts to expire, making them permanent [S2] [S3].

Makes permanent the deduction for higher education expenses, the nonrefundable saver's credit for elective deferrals and IRA contributions, and the increased alternative minimum tax exemption amounts ($49,000 single / $35,750 married) [S2] [S3].
Repeals the section 1202 50 percent exclusion for gain from certain small business stock, folding that benefit into the new flat 15 percent capital gains rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect less revenue, requiring either higher future taxes on others, more borrowing, or larger deficits; middle- and lower-income households gain little because most hold few taxable capital gains, and some savers lose the enhanced small business stock exclusion [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's title and stated purpose frame the capital gains cut as a job-creation measure, but the rate cut is not conditioned on any job creation, and the largest gains accrue to high-income asset holders [S3].

Repealing the sunset of the entire 2001 tax cut act without offsetting revenue would permanently reduce federal receipts, increasing deficits and shifting fiscal pressure onto other programs and future taxpayers [S2] [S3].

Repealing the small business stock exclusion (section 1202) while lowering the general capital gains rate is a trade-off that would change the relative tax treatment of startup and small-business investment versus large public-company holdings [S3].
It is a standalone bill that duplicates what Congress later debated in broader 2003 tax legislation; the capital gains rate was cut to 15 percent in 2003 through a different bill [S1] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits go disproportionately to high-income households with large taxable investment gains, while the cost — foregone federal revenue — is broadly distributed and falls partly on programs serving lower- and middle-income households. The permanent AMT exemption and permanent tuition deduction would help some middle-income households, but the bill's dominant provision is the top capital gains rate cut. The bill was never considered by a committee or chamber, so no vote ever occurred.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died at the end of the 107th Congress in January 2003 without a hearing or vote [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Introduced by Representative Pat Toomey on July 23, 2001, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1] [S5].
No further legislative action was taken; the bill was never reported out of committee, never debated on the House floor, and received no roll call votes in either chamber [S1] [S5].
The bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and was not reintroduced in that Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one: the bill died quietly in committee with no cosponsors and no reported opposition or support. Wealthy investors lost a chance at a lower capital gains rate; the Treasury avoided a large revenue loss, and middle-income households were spared a corresponding fiscal squeeze from permanent extension of the full 2001 tax cut package.

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Toomey (R-PA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote on the bill; it died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party and no floor vote, so no party-split data exists; the sponsor was a conservative Republican and the bill was a Bush-era tax cut extension consistent with that party's agenda, but the record shows only that it attracted no Democratic support and no recorded opposition [S1] [S4].

industries.note: A lower capital gains rate would increase after-tax returns on stocks and investment funds, encouraging investment activity. Ordinary households with 401(k)s or taxable brokerage accounts would also pay less on realized gains, but the largest benefits would accrue to the biggest investors.

The bill repeals the section 1202 exclusion that let founders and early investors in qualified small business stock exclude half their gain, replacing it with a flat 15 percent rate. For small-business holders this is a trade of a targeted benefit for a lower general rate; for the public it removes a tax incentive aimed at early-stage small business investment.

industries.industry: Federal Treasury and general taxpayer base
industries.note: Making the 2001 tax cuts permanent and cutting the capital gains rate would reduce federal revenue, requiring offsetting borrowing or future tax increases elsewhere. The burden of closing that gap would fall on households that do not realize large capital gains.
